name: Chapter 10: Biomolecules
description: Carbohydrates, glucose structure, disaccharides, polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, enzymes, vitamins, nucleic acids, hormones

cards.term: Origin of the name "carbohydrate", and why it fails?
cards.definition: Formula Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ ("hydrates of carbon"); but acetic acid fits and is not one, rhamnose C₆H₁₂O₅ is one but doesn’t fit
Optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds giving these on hydrolysis
Sweet carbohydrates are sugars (sucrose in homes, lactose in milk); saccharide from Greek sakcharon = sugar

cards.text:
Classes by hydrolysis: {{c1::monosaccharides}} (can’t be hydrolysed; ~20 in nature)
{{c2::oligosaccharides}} (2–10 units)
{{c3::polysaccharides}} (many units; not sweet, "non-sugars").

cards.definition: Sucrose → glucose + fructose; maltose → two glucose
Reduce Fehling’s and Tollens’ reagents; all monosaccharides (aldoses and ketoses) are reducing

cards.term: Aldose vs ketose? Naming by carbons?
cards.definition: Aldose: –CHO; ketose: C=O. Carbons prefix: triose, tetrose, pentose, hexose, heptose (e.g. aldohexose)
Free in sweet fruits, honey, ripe grapes; also combined in starch, cellulose, sucrose

cards.term: Glucose from sucrose and from starch?
cards.definition: Sucrose + dil. HCl/H₂SO₄ (alcoholic) → glucose + fructose. Commercially: starch + dil. H₂SO₄ at 393 K, 2–3 atm.
Dextrose an aldohexose probably the most abundant organic compound on earth
n-Hexane: all six C in a straight chain
Oxime and cyanohydrin: a carbonyl group
Gluconic acid (6 C): carbonyl is an aldehyde
Pentaacetate: five –OH on different carbons
Saccharic acid (dicarboxylic): a primary alcohol group

cards.term: Fischer structures of glucose (I), gluconic acid (II), saccharic acid (III)?
cards.definition: Fischer’s configuration

cards.term: Meaning of D and (+) in D-(+)-glucose?
cards.definition: D: configuration (related to D-glyceraldehyde). (+): dextrorotatory. D/L are unrelated to d/l or sign of rotation.
(+)-Glyceraldehyde has –OH on the right (D); (–) on the left (L)

cards.term: Which carbon decides D/L in sugars?
cards.definition: The lowest asymmetric carbon (C-5 in glucose), with the most oxidised carbon written on top

cards.term: α- vs β-glucose: preparation and m.p.?
cards.definition: α: from concentrated solution at 303 K, m.p. 419 K. β: from hot saturated solution at 371 K, m.p. 423 K.

cards.term: How is the cyclic structure formed?
cards.definition: –OH at C-5 adds to –CHO → six-membered cyclic hemiacetal; α and β in equilibrium with open chain

cards.term: What is the anomeric carbon? Anomers?
cards.definition: C-1 (former aldehyde carbon); α and β forms differing only there are anomers

cards.term: What is a pyranose? Haworth structures?
cards.definition: Six-membered ring (like pyran: 1 O + 5 C)

cards.term: Why does glucose pentaacetate lack a free aldehyde? (Intext 10.3)
cards.definition: Acetylation locks C-1 in the cyclic form; the ring can’t open to give –CHO

cards.term: Intuition: why does glucose still give Tollens’ test if mostly cyclic?
cards.definition: The ring is in equilibrium with a small amount of open chain; as it reacts, more ring opens (Le Chatelier)
Ketohexose (C=O at C-2) from sucrose hydrolysis, fruits, honey D-(–)-fructose (laevorotatory)
–OH at C-5 adds to C-2 → five-membered furanose ring (like furan: 1 O + 4 C)
α- and β-D-(–)-fructofuranose
Oxide linkage between two monosaccharides via O, with loss of water
When the reducing groups (–CHO / C=O) of both units are bonded (sucrose); free ones → reducing (maltose, lactose)
C1 of α-D-glucose to C2 of β-D-fructose: non-reducing

cards.term: Why is hydrolysed sucrose called invert sugar?
cards.definition: Rotation changes from dextro (+) to laevo (–): fructose (−92.4°) outweighs glucose (+52.5°)
Two α-D-glucose, C1–C4; free –CHO at C1 of second unit: reducing
β-D-galactose + β-D-glucose, C1 (galactose)–C4 (glucose); reducing (milk sugar)
β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose
Sucrose: α-glucose + β-fructose · C1–C2 · No; Maltose: α-glucose + α-glucose · C1–C4 · Yes; Lactose: β-galactose + β-glucose · C1–C4 · Yes

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Disaccharides

Units · linkage · reducing?

Sucroseα-glucose + β-fructose · C1–C2 · No
Maltoseα-glucose + α-glucose · C1–C4 · Yes
Lactoseβ-galactose + β-glucose · C1–C4 · Yes

cards.definition: Main plant storage polysaccharide cereals, roots, tubers polymer of α-glucose
Water-soluble, 15–20% of starch; unbranched chain of 200–1000 α-D-glucose, C1–C4 links
Water-insoluble, 80–85% of starch; branched: chain C1–C4, branches C1–C6
Only in plants (cell walls), most abundant organic substance in plants; straight chain of β-D-glucose, C1–C4
Animal starch: like amylopectin but more branched in liver, muscles, brain also yeast and fungi

cards.term: Intuition: why can’t humans digest cellulose though it is also glucose?
cards.definition: Its β-linkages need an enzyme (cellulase) we lack; our amylase only cuts α-links

cards.term: Why are glucose and sucrose water-soluble but cyclohexane isn’t? (Intext 10.1)
cards.definition: Many –OH groups H-bond with water

Food, energy (honey in ayurveda), storage (starch, glycogen), cell walls (cellulose), wood, cotton
textiles, paper, lacquers, breweries
ribose and deoxyribose in nucleic acids
Greek proteios: of prime importance. Milk, cheese, pulses, peanuts, fish, meat.
α-Amino acids (–NH₂ on the carbon next to –COOH)

cards.term: Origins of the names glycine and tyrosine?
cards.definition: Glycine: sweet (glykos). Tyrosine: first from cheese (tyros).
Glycine, alanine, valine, leucine
Symbols and side chains
Equal –NH₂ and –COOH: neutral more –NH₂: basic more –COOH: acidic
Essential: cannot be made by the body, must come from diet. Non-essential: synthesised in the body.

cards.text: Essential amino acids (NCERT *): {{c1::valine, leucine, isoleucine}}, {{c2::arginine, lysine}}, {{c3::threonine, methionine}}, {{c4::phenylalanine, tryptophan, histidine}}.

cards.definition: "PVT TIM HALL": Phe, Val, Thr, Trp, Ile, Met, His, Arg, Leu, Lys

cards.term: Why do amino acids behave like salts (high m.p., water-soluble)?
cards.definition: They exist as zwitter ions (–COO⁻ and –NH₃⁺)

cards.term: Why do amino acids melt higher than halo acids? (Intext 10.4)
cards.definition: Zwitter ions: strong ionic attractions
Zwitter ion reacts with both acids and bases

cards.term: Which natural α-amino acid is optically inactive?
cards.definition: Glycine (no asymmetric carbon); others mostly L-configuration (–NH₂ on left)
Amide –CO–NH– from –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of another with loss of H₂O; glycine + alanine → glycylalanine (Gly-Ala)
2, 3 amino acids > 10 = polypeptide > 100 residues, mass > 10,000 u = protein (insulin, 51 residues, still called a protein)
Parallel chains held by H-bonds and disulphide bonds water-insoluble keratin (hair, wool, silk), myosin (muscles)
Chains coil into a sphere usually water-soluble insulin, albumins
The sequence of amino acids; any change creates a different protein
Regular folding by H-bonds between C=O and N–H of the backbone: α-helix or β-pleated sheet
Right-handed screw; each N–H H-bonds to C=O of an adjacent turn
Chains stretched out side by side, held by intermolecular H-bonds (like drapery folds)
Overall folding (fibrous or globular); stabilised by H-bonds, disulphide, van der Waals, electrostatic forces
Spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide sub-units
Primary → secondary → tertiary → quaternary

(a) primary
(b) secondary
(c) tertiary
(d) quaternary
Heat or pH change disturbs H-bonds: globules unfold, helix uncoils, biological activity lost

cards.term: Which structures are lost in denaturation?
cards.definition: Secondary and tertiary destroyed; primary intact
Coagulation of egg white on boiling; curdling of milk (lactic acid from bacteria)

cards.term: Where does egg water go on boiling? (Intext 10.5)
cards.definition: Absorbed/held by the denatured coagulated protein (via H-bonding)
Biocatalysts, almost all globular proteins; very specific for reaction and substrate
After substrate (maltase: maltose → 2 glucose) or reaction (oxidoreductase); ending -ase

cards.term: How do enzymes speed up reactions? Example?
cards.definition: Lower activation energy: sucrose hydrolysis 6.22 kJ/mol with acid vs 2.15 kJ/mol with sucrase
Organic compounds needed in small amounts in diet for specific functions; deficiency causes specific diseases
"Vital amine"; the "e" was dropped since most lack amino groups
A, D, E, K: stored in liver and adipose tissue
B group and C: excreted in urine, must be supplied regularly (except B₁₂, which is stored)
"ADEK": all Dissolve Easily in (K)fat

cards.term: Why can’t vitamin C be stored? (Intext 10.6)
cards.definition: Water-soluble: excreted in urine
Vitamins A–D

cards.term: Sources of vitamins D, E, K?
cards.definition: D: sunlight, fish, egg yolk. E: vegetable oils (wheat germ, sunflower). K: green leafy vegetables.

cards.term: What carries heredity in the nucleus?
cards.definition: Chromosomes: proteins + nucleic acids (DNA, RNA)

cards.term: Why are nucleic acids called polynucleotides?
cards.definition: Long-chain polymers of nucleotides
Pentose sugar + phosphoric acid + nitrogenous bases
DNA: β-D-2-deoxyribose. RNA: β-D-ribose.
DNA: A, G, C, T. RNA: A, G, C, U (uracil replaces thymine).
Purines (two rings): A, G. Pyrimidines (one ring): C, T, U.
Nucleoside: base at 1′ of sugar. Nucleotide: nucleoside + phosphate at 5′.
Phosphodiester between 5′ and 3′ carbons of the sugars
Sugar–phosphate backbone with bases on the sugars

cards.term: Primary structure of a nucleic acid?
cards.definition: The sequence of nucleotides
Double helix: two chains H-bonded via base pairs; strands complementary
A = T and C ≡ G
Single-stranded helix that sometimes folds back
m-RNA, r-RNA, t-RNA

cards.term: Why are RNA base ratios unrelated? (Intext 10.8)
cards.definition: RNA is single-stranded: no complementary pairing

cards.term: Hydrolysis of a DNA nucleotide containing thymine? (Intext 10.7)
cards.definition: 2-Deoxyribose, phosphoric acid, thymine
Nobel 1962 with Crick and Wilkins for the double helix: "a gently twisted ladder"
DNA: reserve of genetic information, self-duplication. RNA: protein synthesis (message from DNA).
Born 1922; Nobel 1968 (with Nirenberg and Holley) for cracking the genetic code
Forensics, paternity, identifying dead bodies, racial groups and evolution
Intercellular messengers from endocrine glands, carried by blood
Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it: together they regulate it
Iodinated derivative of tyrosine low → hypothyroidism (lethargy, obesity, goitre) high → hyperthyroidism iodised salt prevents it
Glucocorticoids: carbohydrate metabolism, inflammation, stress. Mineralocorticoids: water and salt excretion.
Adrenal cortex failure: hypoglycaemia, weakness, stress susceptibility; treated with glucocorticoids + mineralocorticoids
Testosterone (male characters), estradiol (female characters, menstrual cycle), progesterone (prepares uterus)
Sugar: Deoxyribose  |  ribose; Bases: A G C T  |  A G C U; Strands: Double helix  |  single; Function: Heredity, replication  |  protein synthesis

cards.definition: Amylose: α-glucose, C1–C4, unbranched; Amylopectin: α-glucose, C1–C4 + C1–C6 branches; Glycogen: α-glucose, more branched; Cellulose: β-glucose, C1–C4, straight

advancedHtml.backHtml:

Monomer and linkage?

Amyloseα-glucose, C1–C4, unbranched
Amylopectinα-glucose, C1–C4 + C1–C6 branches
Glycogenα-glucose, more branched
Celluloseβ-glucose, C1–C4, straight
